common_name: Alato-Caerulea Passionflower (Fragrant Blue-and-White Hybrid Passion Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun with a trellis or arbor; this old garden hybrid between Passiflora alata and P. caerulea is grown strictly from cuttings since it is largely sterile and sets little to no viable seed.

directions: Plant this old garden hybrid — a cross between Passiflora alata and Passiflora caerulea first raised in the early 1800s — in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun with a trellis or arbor for its vigorous tendrils. The cross combines the size and heavy sweet fragrance of P. alata's flowers with the free-flowering habit and blue-lavender coloring of P. caerulea, producing large blooms with a broad white-and-purple-banded corona over a long summer season. Because the hybrid is largely sterile, expect abundant flowers but little to no viable fruit, so propagate only from stem cuttings rather than seed. In the cooler part of its range the vine dies back to the roots over winter and resprouts vigorously once the soil warms in spring; mulch the crown heavily where marginal.

common_name: Subpeltata Passionflower (Fragrant White Naturalized Passion Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or seed-grown transplants after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; subpeltata passionflower is naturalized throughout much of the Gulf South and self-sows freely where established.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or seed-grown transplants after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade, giving this vigorous South American vine a trellis, fence, or arbor to climb. Passiflora subpeltata bears intensely fragrant, pure white flowers with a fine corona banded in white and pale violet, followed by small, egg-shaped green fruits that ripen to pale yellow and are edible but mild and seedy rather than richly flavored. Naturalized throughout much of the Gulf South and other warm-temperate regions worldwide, it self-sows readily where happy and can spread beyond where it's wanted, so site it where volunteer seedlings are welcome or deadhead spent flowers to limit spread. Like other Passiflora species it serves as a larval host for Gulf fritillary and other heliconian butterflies, and its roots survive brief winter freezes into zone 8 to resprout vigorously each spring.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings well after the last frost, once nights stay reliably warm, in rich, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered site or large container; racemosa passionflower is markedly more cold-sensitive than hardy garden passionflowers and is best moved under cover or into a protected microclimate for winter in zone 9.

directions: Give this Brazilian native a warm, sheltered site with a sturdy trellis or arbor, since Passiflora racemosa is considerably more cold-sensitive than hardy garden passionflowers like maypop or blue passionflower and is best treated as a container plant that can be moved under cover, or planted only in the mildest, most protected corners of a zone 9b-10 garden. Unlike most passionflowers, which bear solitary flowers at each leaf axil, racemosa produces its vivid scarlet-red blooms in pendant, elongating clusters that can each carry a dozen or more flowers over several weeks, making it one of the showiest passionflowers for a warm patio or conservatory. Grow in rich, well-drained soil with light shade during the hottest part of the day to prevent leaf scorch, and water regularly through the growing season while letting the soil dry slightly between waterings in winter. Hummingbirds are frequent visitors to the tubular red flowers, and the vine can be cut back hard in late winter to control size without sacrificing the coming season's bloom.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost against a warm, sheltered wall or fence in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; manicata passionflower comes from cool Andean cloud forests and tolerates brief cold spells better than most scarlet-flowered lowland-tropical passionflowers.

directions: Native to the cool, humid cloud forests of the northern Andes, Passiflora manicata tolerates cooler nights and brief cold spells better than most scarlet-flowered passionflowers from the lowland tropics, making it worth trying against a warm, sheltered wall in a zone 9 Gulf Coast garden. Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun with a trellis or fence, and expect a somewhat shrubbier, less rampant habit than vigorous lowland vines like Passiflora coccinea or P. vitifolia. The brilliant scarlet flowers, each centered with a ring of deep purple-blue filaments, open over a long season and are magnets for hummingbirds. Where winter lows dip into the low 20s F, mulch the root zone heavily and expect topgrowth dieback, with new shoots emerging from the base once temperatures warm in spring.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in a large container once nights stay reliably warm, in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial sun; sanguinolenta passionflower is a compact Andean species best grown on a small patio trellis and moved under cover for winter outside of zone 10-11.

directions: Native to the cloud forests of Ecuador and Peru, Passiflora sanguinolenta is a noticeably more compact, restrained climber than most tropical passionflowers, making it a good fit for a small trellis, hanging basket, or patio container rather than a large arbor. It flowers over a long season with small but intensely colored, blood-red blooms centered by a contrasting corona, and its modest size keeps it manageable for gardeners without room for a sprawling vine. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, grow it as a container plant kept in dappled shade during the hottest part of the day, watering regularly through summer, and bring it under cover or into a bright indoor spot whenever temperatures threaten to fall much below 40 F. Repot every year or two into fresh, humus-rich, well-drained mix to keep the compact root system vigorous.
sources: specialist Passiflora nursery cultivation notes (John Vanderplank, Passiflora Nursery)
